utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technicians, the interpreters. Good morning representatives of the registry, counsel for the Prosecution, the Defence. Good morning, General Krstic. We will continue with the rebuttal of the Prosecutor today in this case in order to complete the testimony which was left incomplete last time. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Defence counsel. We have Mr. Butler. He should be ready to come in, and if we could start off in private session just briefly. The Defence and the Prosecution have been working on some stipulations for -- oh, some for quite a while and some just recently, and I'd like to go over those and tell you about what we have agreed to and what we are offering as additional evidence this morning, somewhat through Mr. Butler, but it should also be brief, if the Court would consider that. But if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in public session, Mr. McCloskey. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would refer the Court to the trial transcripts pages 7392 to 7393 for the particular areas that Mr. Butler's testimony will be rebutting, involves General Krstic's response to questions about his knowledge of when prisoners were first being taken by the VRS. Mr. Butler -- first of all, could we have Exhibit 878A shown to Mr. Butler, as well as if you could provide him with Exhibit 879, which is a map. And as they're getting to those documents, Mr. Butler, was this document and the following document, which is 877, were they part of your initial narrative and your study in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were material that I had looked at but that I had not included in my narrative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Given what these issues discuss now, they probably should have been, and I would suspect that I just missed them in the process of collating all the material around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did these two documents come from? How did they come into OTP possession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exhibit 878 was a document that was seized from the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade during a search by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we could get 877 ready for him also. And you know what 877 is, the daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, same circumstances; it came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor as part of that same search.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you could, and if you need to use the ELMO to help illustrate it, can you just explain briefly this document and how it fits into your analysis and especially where it refers to prisoners being taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This particular document is an intelligence report, a report from the assistant commander -- or assistant chief of staff for intelligence of the Zvornik Brigade, Captain Dusko Vukotic to the command of the Drina Corps, and if I slide that down, you can see that better. It's to their intelligence section. What this document does is gives the Drina Corps intelligence section a breakdown of the situation in the zone of the Zvornik Brigade as the intelligence officer of the Zvornik Brigade understands it. In this case, he's getting the majority of the information that he's receiving from intercepting of Muslim communications from the various segments of the column, the advanced part of the column, the second part of the column, then the main body of the column, which is still to the south. Relevant to prisoners, what this document indicates down at the last three lines or last four or five lines is the fact that they talk about a third group of prisoners being discovered in the -- third group of individuals in the area of Bokcanski Potok. He notes that the individuals are fleeing in panic without any control and, in groups or individually, they are giving themselves up to the MUP or the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you now use the map, Exhibit 879, and put it on the ELMO and just give the Court a brief outline of the -- where Bokcanski Potok is and where the intelligence people feel the various parts of the column are at the time of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time of this document, which was drafted on the 12th but not physically received by the Drina Corps until 1.00 in the morning on the 13th, the situation, as they understood it, was that the main elements or the -- the advanced elements of the column were in this area here, moving out. Another larger group of armed soldiers from the column --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, if you could just say where it is, for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through the Caparde and Spreca valley. The second element of the column which consisted of what they called approximately 300 or 400 armed people moving up through the greater Kamenica area, which is Redzici, Velja Glava. Then the third series of the column, which was the main body of the column, the very long part in this area referred to as Bokcanski Potok which is an area that we frequently call -- it's the other side of the road from the Sandici meadow in Kravica area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to Exhibit 877. If you could briefly describe -- we've seen many of these documents but how does -- does this document help identify units that may be in the area where prisoners are being taken on 12 July by -- according to the document we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This specific document is the 12 July 1995 combat report, the regular combat report to the commander of the Drina Corps from the command of the 1st Zvornik Brigade, and in paragraph 2, discusses the primary tasks for the units and, in that, the brigade chief of staff, in this case Dragan Obrenovic, lays out where elements of both the brigade and -- to include some of the military police assets of the brigade are located in ambush positions relative to where they believe the column is approaching or where the Muslim armed forces are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if there is one military police detachment sent to Konjevic Polje, that would be roughly in what area, looking at the map just to remind us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Going back to the map, Konjevic Polje area is right where the turn comes off from the road from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje and then going down towards Milici. It is a major intersection area. And as previous witness and my own testimony has indicated, that was a -- one of the collection sites for Muslims who were being collected. They had made it further up the road as they were crossing the road from Konjevic Polje to Milici. As they crossed that highway, those that were caught, many were held in Konjevic Polje, others were held in Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those -- that happened on the 13th that we know of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The major captures of the Muslims took place on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this exhibit, the daily combat report on 877A notes about the military police detachment sent to Konjevic Polje, and it says, "... pursuant to your order." So what is -- can you tell us, "pursuant to your order," who do you take that to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As broad as it is, I would take that to be pursuant to an order from the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Visnjic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let me go back to this last document. It is the daily combat report of the 12th of July 1995. Who compiled this daily combat report, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These daily combat reports would have been compiled by the -- by procedure, it should have been the operations duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The signature is the commander, Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic. Was his presence confirmed during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During this period, Colonel Pandurevic was down in the area of Srebrenica. The reports in question were -- this one is not signed, but the majority of the reports during this period were signed for him by the chief of staff, now Major Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did your investigations show a hypothetical assignment that this group from the Zvornik Brigade - and it is a department of the military police - was to have executed in the Konjevic Polje area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm confused about the word that translated into English as a "hypothetical."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase that. Did your investigation ascertain the assignments that this group had in Konjevic Polje, and I'm referring to the group of the -- that is to say, the military police department, detachment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Putting it in context with the intercepts that we have, which I think several of them pertain to police units in the area of Konjevic Polje, the two options are, one, combat-related activity to defend that intersection from the column, or the second one would be a traditional military police function of dealing with the prisoner issues. But at this point, I'm not able to say exactly what the function was. It does not specify an ambush function like it does in the previous one on a military police platoon, but again, I can't specify what the function was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me assist you. Could one function be the establishment of a checkpoint for the control of traffic, for example, vehicles moving in that direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is an option and, again, given other information that, on the 13th, checkpoints were established there, it is a viable option, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: That means, then, that we have three possible options at this stage of our exchange of opinions, if I can put it that way; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, let me go back to a series of questions briefly that was put by my learned colleague, Mr. McCloskey. Without any specific details, the Polje at Sandici, the Sandici meadow, we identified a tank which was within the composition of the MUP units. We identified the soldiers as well who were also MUP members. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers, as we discussed earlier, yes. Again, the issue was a compilation of both MUP and soldiers. As for the issue of the tank, that one individual identifies it as a MUP tank, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: But we have a precise identification only for the MUP members. So far you haven't identified any of the members of the army; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, in the events at Jadar, a member of MUP was also identified. Now, my question is: Was a member of the Drina Corps identified who took part in those events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be clear on that, I'm not sure of the answer. I just don't recall the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the Branjevo farm events, the members of the 10th Diversionary Detachment were identified and, in your previous testimony, those of another unit which I don't want to specify now because we're in open session, so I won't be mentioning that unit. But was a member of the Bratunac Brigade identified? Just give us a yes or no answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask the registry to give the witness and members of the Prosecution Exhibit D165, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, before we move on to this exhibit and to give a chance to the Prosecution to look through the document, I would like to ask you the following: During your testimony in the Prosecution case, you spoke about the use of MUP by -- that is to say, in the combat activities in the Srebrenica enclave and the Krivaja 95 operation; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You also in your testimony mentioned that one of the -- what led you to believe this at one point was that the MUP forces were mentioned in the Operation Krivaja 95 as reserve forces. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You also in the course of your testimony, the main part of your testimony, you said that the MUP forces were used by the army of Republika Srpska, but that you did not have a document which directly indicates that order; that is to say, you don't have the order of the Drina Corps on the deployment of those forces. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I do not have a document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the units who were located on the line Konjevic Polje-Bratunac, were they MUP units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were a mixture of both MUP and army, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What about the units that provided security for this axis, Konjevic Polje-Bratunac; were they also a mixture of MUP and army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I've been able to put together based on the documents and the recent interviews, and of course I won't go into detail, is that the line as it extended was the units closest to Bratunac were the 1st Battalion Bratunac Brigade. The units that extended up from the area of -- and perhaps it's better if I use the map on this one. This location being Bratunac, and again, here the intersection of Konjevic Polje, in this segment closer to Bratunac is the 1st Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade, and then you go up to the area of Glogova, from the area of Glogova through Kravica, and a little beyond is the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade which, as identified earlier, is also the 8th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. It was performing duty as part of the Bratunac Brigade at that time. And then from beyond that, from the area between Sandici and Konjevic Polje, what we've been able to determine is at least the 1st Company of the police, the Special Police intervention unit that came out of CSB Zvornik, as well as some elements of the Special Police Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, on the 13th of July in the afternoon hours at the positions between Konjevic Polje and Glogova -- or Konjevic Polje and Bratunac, to take it further afield, on the 13th of July, were members identified, members of these two battalions, the Bratunac Brigade, on that route, road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... recent interviewees that we've done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I mean your investigations, were you able to come up with that, that on that road there were members of these two battalions on the 13th of July in the afternoon? You can give us a yes or no answer again; we don't need the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like the witness to be able to explain, if he needs to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Visnjic. The question -- you were asked to give a yes or no answer, but if you wish to explain, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is, as part of the investigation, in the case of the 1st Battalion, yes; in the case of the 4th Battalion, the documents reflect that, not a physical aspect of the investigation. As in the case of the MUP, that's part of the physical investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, was one of the tasks of the 1st Battalion to move from the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road southwards into the depth of the territory and, in fact, to leave the road, get away from the road, in the period between the 12th and 13th, and especially on the afternoon of the 13th of July? Am I correct in saying this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, I should now like to ask you to look at the document that you have before you, it is Defence Exhibit D165, but one more question before we go on to the document. You know the assertion by the Defence that the units which controlled the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road were outside the chain of command of the Drina Corps. You know that we say that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, there was some discussion about that, and Defence witnesses were questioned as well as Prosecution witnesses on that particular issue. I should now like to ask you to look at document 165A.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a document, Mr. President, which the Defence came by directly prior to this meeting, this sitting, and the document has been translated. If our colleagues of the Prosecution have any comments to make with respect to the translation, we will -- we are ready to accept this, but it is a document which was issued by the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, and it is signed by the chief of the intelligence department, General Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, first of all, could I ask you to peruse the document before we go on to my concrete questions. I'm sure you need a few moments to look at it, and as do my learned colleagues of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I've not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, does this document correspond to the standard form used for documents with this kind of contents compiled by the organs of the Republika Srpska army in the course of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part, it does; however, the one anomaly that I would note is that usually as part of the header data -- and probably to make that clear to everybody, this is the information that I refer to as the header data, who it's to and under what circumstances, to or for information. Generally the date is there, and on this document, we don't see the date at that part; however, there is a date of 12 July on the back as well as an order number. Normally, we see those at the front, and that would leave me a bit of a question. But other than those things, it is a pretty standard format.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in view of the format of this document, am I right in saying that this document was compiled by Major General Zdravko Tolimir, in those days member of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this particular case, it was certainly released under his signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying, Mr. Butler, that this document was issued on the 12th of July 1995 and that it reached the command of the 2nd Romanija Motorised Brigade on that same day at 2210 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that's -- it certainly reached the command of the Romanija Brigade, 2nd Romanija Brigade at that time. So given all of that, I would say -- I would be pretty comfortable saying that it's the 12th of July, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Am I also right in saying that the document was registered in the book of records the next day, the 13th of July 1995, as can be seen from the stamp on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's consistent with the practice, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this document was sent to several addressees. Among others, one of the addressees is the forward command post at Pribicevac, to General Krstic in person. My question is whether, on the 12th of July 1995 late in the evening, the forward command post at Pribicevac was operational?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that it is my opinion, and it is the Prosecution's contention, that the forward command post at Pribicevac did remain operational during this period. I do not believe that it shut down, consistent with some of the Defence witnesses, at midnight or earlier on the evening of the 11th. I believe it remained operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And according to your contention, until when did that forward command post continue to operate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that, consistent with some of the exhibits that were forwarded either through my testimony or through the cross-examination of General Krstic, there is one particular order there dated the 13th of July that is also addressed to the forward command post at Pribicevac and I do not know the number of that exhibit, unfortunately. So it's my contention that certainly the Drina Corps headquarters had an understanding that on the 13th of July, the forward command post at Pribicevac was still in some form of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The documents were addressed to the forward command post at Pribicevac, but do you have any evidence to show that they were received there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 13th, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that during the cross-examination of one of the witnesses, I believe who was a protected witness so I will not mention his name, the Prosecution forwarded a document that was received late evening, early morning hours of 12 July. I believe it was the late evening of the 11th to the early morning of the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler -- let me withdraw that. Is that the only piece of evidence on the basis of which you assume that this forward command post was operating or, rather, receiving documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the document before you, Defence Exhibit D165, consists of two parts, if I can call them that. In the first, there is a description of information based on an interview with a prisoner of war. I should like to draw your attention to the second part of this document which begins, in fact, on page 2. Particularly the first paragraph of the document, which reads: "We have informed Ministry of Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska organs who are stationed in Konjevic Polje with the legal corridor through which the Muslims of Srebrenica are breaking through considering that they have the assignment to secure the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje communication." Is that statement correct or true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that -- notwithstanding the truthfulness of the translation, I will assume that's accurate. But I'm aware that during the period there was in fact a small MUP detachment at Konjevic Polje. I do not believe that they had the entire -- they had the job of -- they had the role of securing the entire line of communication between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje. It's an awful long stretch of road, and there weren't that many MUP formations there. I think it would be pretty impossible for them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if we look at page 1 and see to whom the document was addressed, the MUP of Republika Srpska and RDB, in the Defence submission, that is the Department of State Security of the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska. Would you agree with me in my interpretation of this abbreviation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that's an accurate interpretation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Why, Mr. Butler, would the Main Staff, the supreme body, give orders to a small MUP unit in Konjevic Polje to secure the communication line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if you look at this document in its entirety, not only who it was sent to and, again, first when you look at the header information, the first individuals that it was sent to, the primary customer, so to speak, was the Drina Corps command. And, again, looking at it if you look at -- as you've noted on the second page, if you look in the second paragraph below the yellow highlighted one, it also discusses the duty of the brigade command to inform the Department of Public Safety and Security. I believe, again, when you look at this in its entirety, this is consistent with the fact that, you know, my belief as to my analysis and I believe as the Prosecution's issue as well is that, during this period, that the MUP forces are operating under army command and control. And this document, particularly the second period, reflects that. The army was the first person on the addressee list and, in this case, given the fact that the MUP are the last people down the line, certainly the army formations were the first intended recipients of it, specifically, in this case, General Krstic and Lieutenant Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, it is the submission of the Defence that the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road was controlled by the MUP either through the special brigade or other MUP units. Can this document be said to fit into the submission of the Defence as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking at the first and the second paragraphs of page 2 and using those as the basis, I would say that it doesn't. And the reason that I don't believe it does is the fact that the brigade commands are being told through their organs of intelligence affairs to propose to the commanders the measures to undertake to prevent the illegal breakthrough of the Muslims. Putting paragraphs 1 and 2 on page 2 together, I don't believe it supports that contention. Now, again, if you look at paragraph 1 in isolation, it would support that contention.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, can it be seen from this document that the MUP was subordinated to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe that this document specifically states that the MUP is subordinate to the Drina Corps. However, I believe that you can get a feel for that, and that's a weak word, but you can get a feel for that by looking at paragraph 3 where it specifically discusses the issue that the Bratunac, Zvornik and Milici Brigades, in collaboration with the local departments of public security in their areas of responsibility are to organise the traffic through some of the key routes that they knew that the column would be crossing over. So while it does not specifically state that, I believe that looking at that third paragraph, you could get an inclination of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, your knowledge of the word "collaboration" or "cooperation," does that indicate subordination or does cooperation mean something else, the meaning attributed to the word by the Prosecution when interpreting certain other documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word, and this is kind of fuzzy because it's, again, the translation, and that's where it gets unclear. The phrase it's normally done is "cooperation." I'm assuming that in this particular translation, "collaboration" and "cooperation" are the same word for the purpose of the translation. In this particular case what I look at this is looking at it in the form of the brigades to cooperate and, in the sense of the JNA doctrine, cooperation does not specifically mean command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, does the Prosecution possess any document except for the Krivaja 95 plan from which it would be possible to find in writing which would -- or rather which would describe the relationship of the Drina Corps command over MUP units and specifically over MUP units stationed along the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac communication line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a 15 July -- I believe it's 15 or 16 July 1995 daily combat report from the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade where the brigade commander sends a report up to the Drina Corps where he specifically talks about the fact that the MUP forces there have withdrawn, and he's not sure by whose order that they've left, but because of that, now his forces have got to go cover that line. That is the only other document other than Krivaja 95 Op plan which discusses that issue of the MUP and the army and the subordination with the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you will agree with me that that order is dated the 16th of July. I looked at it yesterday. It is a regular combat report of the Bratunac Brigade, dated the 16th of July. To be quite clear, in the period of the 11th, 12th, and 13th of July when the certain events occurred along the route Konjevic Polje-Bratunac, is there any single document specifying the command relationship of the Drina Corps over the MUP, either as special Brigades or any MUP units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During that period, there is not a physical document, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, even if you were to consider the first paragraph only of this document, which shows that the Main Staff is in a certain sense setting assignments to the MUP, be it a small unit as you allege or the entire MUP unit as submitted by the Defence ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is that a question, sir? It kind of hung off on the transcriber.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Allow me to repeat it, Mr. Butler. If we look at the first paragraph on page 2 of Exhibit D165, even if we were to view it in isolation as you are suggesting, is that the only evidence of the fact that the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska is allegedly controlling the MUP, or that the Main Staff is in a certain sense issuing assignments to MUP units or is familiar with the assignments of MUP units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree with the latter interpretation you gave it, that is, familiar with the assignments of the MUP units, by virtue of the fact that in the first paragraph it notes that, "We have informed the organs of the Ministry of the Interior Affairs," and it specifies they're not -- that they're not tasking them, "them" being the Main Staff is not tasking them. And again, considering this is coming from the intelligence department and not from operations, it would be inappropriate for them to be tasking as such. So I would agree with your second interpretation, that they're certainly aware of the MUP presence in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, who did the MUP report to about its activities in Konjevic Polje and along the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on the recent series of interviews, and again I won't go into detail on that, the individuals in question continue to essentially indicate that they reported up through their MUP channels to at least as far as Colonel Borovcanin, who we've identified in previous testimony as the commander of the MUP forces on the ground in that area. The next link over would be Colonel Borovcanin reporting to the local army commands, and in that particular case, we do not have any physical evidence that establishes that linkage other than their proximity presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, do you have any evidence to show the opposite, that is, that the command of the Drina Corps was not familiar with the activities of MUP units along the Konjevic-Bratunac communication line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. Most of the information I have indicates that the Drina Corps units had an awareness, certainly in the intercepts and certainly in other documents, that they were aware of the activities of the MUP all through that period. Intercepts of the 12th and of the 13th and some on the 14th are pretty clear that they're currently coordinating their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, who was the commander of the Drina Corps on the 13th of July in the afternoon hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my contention, based on the signed order from General Krstic as the commander of the Drina Corps, that I believe the order of time is sometime between 1730 and 2000 hours, and again, my memory has slipped on that one but, based on that signed order, I believe that General Krstic was the commander of the Drina Corps in that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is getting beyond the scope into some issues that if Mr. Butler -- if they wish to reopen and they wish to go into this with Mr. Butler, if at least he could have the documents present to help refresh his recollection. But I -- this is -- I would object to any further -- going further afield.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was going to raise that particular issue. I think that Mr. Butler discussed this issue at length, as you know, and to go back to it, perhaps he should have the document in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is just an introductory question to the question that comes next, but to refresh Mr. Butler's memory, I should like to ask the registry to provide him with document 525, Prosecution Exhibit 525.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is an interview carried out on the 13th of July at 1829 hours -- or rather, a conversation, I'm sorry, between Zile and an X, and during your examination-in-chief, during the Prosecution case, you identified one of these two participants in the conversation as General Zivanovic. In the course of this conversation, mention is made, a list -- made of a list of prisoners of war -- no, I'm sorry, a list of potential war criminals which General Zivanovic is requesting from the other participant in the conversation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just take a minute to read this again, please. Okay, your question again, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In this conversation, reference is made to a list of suspected war criminals which, as far as I can remember, General Zivanovic is requesting to be given to him for the purposes of an investigation. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to counsel's conclusion. I think that this clearly is not established, who this is, conclusively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. McCloskey, but I think that we have Mr. Richard Butler here who will answer that question. Perhaps it would be a good idea to show the document on the ELMO, please, so that we can see it. Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my question is on the monitor, on the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So am I right, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Zile" is a nickname that we associate with General Zivanovic, yes, sir. Let me just go back to the transcript here and make sure there's nothing of part of the question that I missed. And yes, as part of that, the individual Zile is requesting a list of war criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, should we hypothetically assume that this conversation is authentic, that a participant in the conversation is General Zivanovic, that MUP units are under the command of the Drina Corps, would it be possible that at 1820 [as interpreted], a time which the Prosecution contends - I'm sorry, it should be 1829 for the LiveNote, not 1820 - a time when, according to the contention of the Prosecution, the killings in Jadar, in Cerska, had already occurred, and most probably also the killings began or underway -- or are underway at Kravica, how would it be possible for General Zivanovic, the commander of the Drina Corps, not to know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking through the LiveNote transcript, there are two issues in that question, and I think maybe the best way for me to answer it is to go over each of them, the first one being General Zivanovic is the commander. And again, as I've indicated, I don't believe by this period of time he is the commander of the Drina Corps based on the other documents. And certainly this intercept is an indicator that he may be. There are other intercepts that have him in discussions with Colonel Vukotic later that evening that I believe on cross-examination you've raised it. Those are indicators that he may well be in command. My view is that he's not in command, that General Krstic is in command of the Drina Corps, based on the written orders. So that's the first part of the question. As for the second issue of the question, how could General Zivanovic not know, given this time frame of what was happening; I don't know the answer to that. I don't know how anyone in the Drina Corps could not have known about what was going on, given the scope and the scale. So it would be my contention that General Zivanovic probably did know at least some components of it, just as members of the Drina Corps all knew some components of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I think we need a break. Are you about to finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, another five minutes, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, then. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the first order signed by General Krstic, was it signed at 2030 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You'll have to give me the order on that one. I just don't recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It is Prosecution exhibit ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And if I could make it a little easier, perhaps. I believe that the window I used was the last order that was signed by General Zivanovic on the 13th of July, was 1730, and then the order -- I believe you're correct, it is in fact 2030 signed by General Krstic. I believe that that's the window that I use to make the conclusion that between that 1730 hours and 2030 hours is when the change of command probably occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Within that time period, General Zivanovic is nonetheless conducting a conversation, an active conversation, a kind of conversation that would be expected from a Corps Commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly an active conversation expected of someone who is a General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, according to the contention of the Prosecution or, rather, the hypothesis of the Prosecution, General Krstic and General Zivanovic were together during that time period; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that during that time period, the general body of evidence used by the Prosecution put General Mladic, General Krstic and General Zivanovic together during some portion of that time period and that is, in fact, the change of command. That is the event that occurs at the Vlasenica headquarters on the 13th. So I believe we have all three principals there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, General Zivanovic, at least that can be concluded from the conversation conducted on -- at 1829 hours, is not aware of the listed and mentioned events Jadar, Cerska and probably Kravica; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those events are not listed in the contents of this conversation, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, just one more question. In view of the document you have in front of you, which is Defence Exhibit D165, and the document tendered by the Prosecution as OTP Exhibit 877, could it be concluded that one of the assumptions as to why this unit or detachment of the military police was sent to Konjevic Polje was precisely to regulate traffic, as stated on paragraph 3 on page 2 of Exhibit 165 of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one part where I have some difficulty in concluding that is the fact that given in Exhibit 877 which is the 12 July combat report and, again, that report was sent -- if I can find my English language translation -- at 1710 hours, and this one from the intelligence director of the Main Staff wasn't sent from 2210. So based on the fact that the Main Staff document comes out many hours after the daily combat report, and the fact that they have received the order prior to putting in the daily combat report at 1710, I'm not sure you can make a direct linkage to that. There are many documents that we have dated the 12th and 13th that have been tendered into evidence which talk about the setting up of checkpoints and everything else, and I think those are probably more tied to 877 than Defence 165 is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Visnjic. We are now going to have a half-hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, will there be any additional questions for this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a few.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- as regards the issue of Zile Zivanovic. You made an objection and I thought that you would have an opportunity to react if you think it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That was one of the issues I just wanted Mr. Butler to review.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Butler, could we go to Exhibit 525A. I hope you've still got that in front of you, and if you could make sure the whole thing is on the ELMO. Have you had a chance to carefully read this and review what you had said about it previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, what can you tell us about who is speaking and -- in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this particular intercept, it's clear that they only have one side of the conversation. And they make it clear that the individual identified as Zile is not audible. So you have this subscriber that's on the other hand of the conversation. You do not have Zile himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So this line down the page, "Let me explain what's happening, call me in the morning. We'll fucking miss them and they'll get away scot free." In your opinion, is that Zivanovic or Zile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, that's the other subscriber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you have any idea who this person is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if you -- I want to ask you about two intercepts very briefly, and I've shown the Defence which ones we want to talk about there. One is a July 12 intercept. It's Exhibit 364, July 12, tab -- can you tell us the tab?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's tab 4, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you put that on the ELMO. Now, just again, briefly, what can you tell us about this on the issue of municipal police and who they may be taking orders from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this conversation, again, the subscriber is Obrenovic, and it discusses the fact that, listen, please, I call them -- that Mane will call him, and that the police in Konjevic Polje have been told to do the same as the Engineer Battalion is doing, that he can give orders to them through the commander of the Engineering Battalion. So in this regards, this puts the civilian municipal police receiving their orders through the commander of the army Engineering Battalion at Konjevic Polje. That's the 5th Engineering Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the 5th Engineering Battalion, as we recall, is a Drina Corps asset?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, was Witness S interrogated by people in camouflage uniforms in front of the headquarters and COMS building of the 5th Engineering Battalion on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that is his testimony, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we can go to the next intercept that I've asked you to look at, it's the July 13 intercept in the same exhibit, 364, July 13 in the evening, between Krstic and Borovcanin. And what tab is that, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, could you tell us the number of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, this is 364/1, and then it goes by date, July 13th, tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe there's a tab number listed on this one, unless it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the grey tab.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sixteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Tab 16. And again, can you just briefly remind us the context of this, who these people are, and how it fits into this issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a conversation between the two subscribers, one of them General Krstic, one of them is a Borovcanin who we understand Ljubo Borovcanin was the person in charge of the police activities relative to Potocari and the general area of Srebrenica. And in this conversation, Krstic is calling Borovcanin, asking him where he is at the command post, and essentially, you know, wanting to determine whether or not he has any problems. And again, Borovcanin says he does not. He tells Krstic that he doesn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you view this militarily? Can you give any indication of the relationship between these two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe, as I said in my direct testimony pertaining to this one, to me, this is an indication that Borovcanin is functioning under the command and control of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to the Defence Exhibit 165 from Tolimir of the Main Staff to General Krstic, Lieutenant Colonel Popovic, and other units. And I notice in the bottom of the first paragraph the prisoner -- they say, "The prisoner estimates that on 11 July this year within Zulfo's group, about 500 armed Muslims left. Among them were also military-capable unmarried women and children." Do you know why the Main Staff would be interested in military-capable children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you, after studying this document, provide your opinion as to who would have captured this individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In looking at this document, the -- and I'm sorry, I have to pull it off the screen here. I can't read it from the ELMO. In the very first series of lines of the first paragraph, it discusses that on 12 July at 1800 hours on the road Bratunac-Kravica in the region of the village of Kajici, a member was captured. That village is the headquarters of the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade which, again, is also the 8th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. Given those -- the fact that where he was captured as well as the kind of questions that are being asked of him as to where the Muslim military formations are, my conclusion is that the individual was captured by the army, not by the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just have one question you may be in a position to give me a satisfactory answer. You're adamant in your conclusion that -- you said exactly: "Most information indicate that Drina Corps had an awareness of the activities of the MUP and that they were currently coordinating their activities together, so let us consider that the bottom line was that they were aware, the Drina Corps was aware of the MUP activity." Now, how far would the Drina Corps command be entitled to use a veto, to use a modern word, to use a veto against activities of the MUP, when -- if they are aware of what they are doing? Could they tell them, "No, don't do that," granting this is the bottom line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they should have been able to do that. The legislation on when the MUP comes under army command is fairly clear on the fact that once MUP units are subordinated to the army, that they fall under the command of the brigade and corps commanders in that zone. The only specific limitations on the army commander resolves around not using the MUP outside of the agreed framework of what they were sent to do and the fact that the army commander cannot replace the MUP commander of that unit. It still has to remain under MUP actual command. Other than that, and given the fact that the army would command those units within the zone, certainly if the MUP function -- or the MUP formation were doing something outside of what the army deemed was necessary, appropriate, or part of the plan, the army certainly could have made their views known that this activity had to stop, and enforce that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So in the last analysis, the army of the Drina Corps had to okay the activity of the MUP, to give -- if the consent is not given, they cannot act, and they can't tell them no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For those specific functions that they were put under army control. For other civilian policing type of functions, it's a different story, but when they're specifically put under the army control, they have that veto, as you use, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And what would you call policing functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The normal municipal police functions: crime enforcement, local security of the population in Milici area and those types of areas. Their traditional police functions. When they're mobilised, there's a special unit, so to speak, and placed under army command. For example, their use along the roads, that's not a traditional police function. In that case, they're being used as a police formation under army command, and in those functions, they do that. But for normal police functions, I would say that, yeah, the army doesn't necessarily have a voice in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the police functions would be the normal police functions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: -- which have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which have nothing to do with military operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, three questions. One is a little bit more specific version of the area you were talking to Judge Riad about. Even if in your understanding of VRS rules and regulations, et cetera, even if a civilian MUP had been assigned the task of securing a road, would they conceivably have had the authority when capturing people on that road, given the fact that these people we have been told again and again were looked upon as part of the follow-up of the 28th Muslim army, would they -- or can you think of a conceivable source of authority for the MUP having secured the road and captured people on the road to themselves dispose of captured prisoners of war, not handing them over to the army, even if they had been given that -- given the task of securing that road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, ma'am. Most of the information that I had indicates that the army was the primary proponent agency for prisoners of war, again, with a view to collecting the individuals and exchanging them for captured soldiers that the Muslim side or the Croat side had. In that regard, I don't have anything that would indicate that the MUP, of their own, would dispose of prisoners and not turn them over to the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Would they have had any authority to do so, to your knowledge? Could they have hustled them all off to the local gaol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Limited numbers could have been hustled off but at any points in time the gaols, presumably, would have been full. Could they have collected them on their side and not tell anybody? No. And, in fact, there are exhibits that have been tendered which indicate from the army that these prisoners are supposed to be put under custody and taken and held in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: And had they treated them -- we're in supposition now. Had they treated them as civilians captured in what you might say were ordinary police activities, they would have -- would they not have had to go through regular civilian kinds of justice procedures in order to dispose of them legally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The only procedure that I'm aware of, and I believe I discussed this a little bit in my direct testimony, where the police are the primary proponent are those individuals who have been identified as potential war criminals in which case they fall under the purview of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. I have two very quick questions on one of your main exhibits, 877A, just to put what you've talked about into context. There are two other references in paragraph 2 under command of the Drina Corps which is on page 1 that I just wish you might tell me what you think they were talking about. One is the third little dash down, "All other units have made preparations and intensified vigilance against possible arrival of Turks behind our back." Who are they talking about there? Are they talking about the regular Muslim army? Who are they talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, ma'am. In this case they're talking about the column. As indicated in earlier testimony, they started gaining an awareness very early as to this column coming up. They were arrayed against the Muslim forces of 2 Corps on the front line, and they were extremely concerned about the fact that they did not have a whole lot of reserve forces and that this large armed column would literally be approaching their positions from the rear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. So that may be read as saying that they have all their units on some kind of -- other units that haven't been given other designations, on vigilance again the column, against the arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: The other one is two dashes down. This one we're now talking about is on the 12th of July, and they said, "We sent to Bratunac, pursuant to your order, eight buses from Drinatrans, two buses from Praga, and four of our trucks." What context do you put that in, this being the 12th? Is this part of the original commandeering of buses or does this mean these buses have been deflected from some of their women and children escort over to Bratunac to pick up the men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, ma'am. I believe this is in relation to the original call from the Drina Corps for buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Mr. Butler, I also have a question for you, but I am somewhat concerned that -- how to put it -- that I will not be able to formulate it very clearly, but you might be able to help me. You have spoken about the document 165. You mentioned the village of Kajici in the first paragraph, and you told us that the Bratunac Brigade was the one that was there. Did I understand you correctly, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The unit in question is the 4th Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade. Where it gets somewhat confusing is that same unit is also the 8th Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade, and because there was always a manpower shortage in the Bratunac area, what occurred some time in the late 1993 time period was that the 8th Battalion from the Zvornik Brigade was attached to, on a long-term attachment, to the Bratunac Brigade to cover that period -- cover that stretch of the road and around the enclave because they did not have the manpower. So the brigade, the battalion functioned under the command and control of the Bratunac Brigade; however, it was organic to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at the document D165 and the Prosecution Exhibit 877, if we look at both these documents together, we see that they both are dated the 12th of July. The document number 877, in the second paragraph, which starts with the words, "Primary tasks for units," we see further down, in the fourth paragraph where we can read, I will read it in English [In English], "to the area of the 8th in Kajici." [Interpretation] Does that give you a new element? Can that be considered as a confirmation for what you have just said? How do you view it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I view it as confirming what I've just said, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So finally I didn't actually have a question, but thank you anyway for helping me understand this issue. We will have no further questions for you, Mr. Butler. Thank you once again for coming here. Let me just wish you a lot of success in your future work. Mr. Usher will show you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I think that there are some documents to be tendered into evidence by you and by the Defence as well. Please let us hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have the first of all the stipulations, 890, 891, and 892. And then we have 877, 878, the two July 12 reports; 879, the map. And Ms. Keith tells me we have also -- there's an old intercept from a while back that Bogicevic/Zivanovic intercept which has not been dealt with, but it may be dealt with on the matters which was for that other subject. So I would offer the six exhibits into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the intercept Bogicevic/Zivanovic, has it been marked for identification? Does it have a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 884A and B and we have no objection to that intercept going into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no objections as regards to documents 890, 891, and 892, the stipulations, that is. 877, 878, and 879, however, the Defence believes that they should be discussed and dealt with together with a number of objections that we have made as regards similar evidence which has been presented by the Prosecution. As for 884A and B, it is a new piece of evidence, that is, the intercept which was mentioned during the testimony of Ms. Frease, the Defence has no objection to that document. However, on the other hand, the Defence would like to tender 160B, A and B, I apologise, with certain conditions. Sorry, I apologise, my mistake, 165A and B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. McCloskey, I don't know whether you wish to reply to the objection which was made by the Defence concerning 877 through 879, and also I don't know whether you wish to state your opinion regarding Defence Exhibit 165.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Regarding 877, 878, and 879, that issue has been fairly fully briefed on paper. You have received our response to their motion to exclude it so I don't think anything more need be said on that unless you have any particular questions. As for the new Defence document, D165A, we would like to have a chance to get an official translation of that. We also would like to hear where it came from. Some kind of foundation, I think we have a foundation witness, perhaps that witness can help us, but just some sort of indication that it has some indicia of reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we've been deluged with paper of late, so I'm sure it's covered some place in your paper, but remind me, on the 877 to 879, July 12th intercepts, you've told us or Mr. Butler has told us that, well, just going through the first time, they were there but he didn't realise their significance or that sort of thing. Are you now tying those to something very specific in the Defence case or is it more of a general argument? I know you've told us on paper but I honestly --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, the -- they are extremely specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: That was the questioning on the cross-examination of General Krstic or it was Judges' question. It was my question. I've been trying to get you to say that, Mr. McCloskey, but I wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We quoted the exchange between you and General Krstic in our papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I thought, but I needed to be reassured that was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was very clear that he did not have any information about prisoners being taken in the 12-17 time frame in response to your specific questions and that is what we -- when we found these documents, we realised they were of importance and so we wanted to bring them into the rebuttal case, and that's what they are for. The first document is very specific to your question. The second document is -- provides the identity of one of the units of the VRS that was doing the -- was in that area that may have been involved in prisoners, and also additionally rebuts the Defence claim that the Drina Corps was not in that area involved in this process. That is more of a general rebutting on the second one, but it -- so it provides context to the first document and is a general rebuttal also. So I don't have anything else to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of the reservations made by Mr. McCloskey, that is the official translation of the document, source of authenticity, is there anything that you wish to add, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as regards the official translation, of course we agree that the Prosecution be given some additional time while waiting for the official translation of the document. As regards the source of the document, I think I have two options. I can inform you about the source of the document now, or during the break I can inform the Prosecution about the source of the document and if they agree with the document, maybe they will withdraw the objection. So we have two possibilities. It's up to my learned colleague Mr. McCloskey to decide, and I will do as he sees it fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, in response to what Mr. Visnjic has just told us concerning the authenticity of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think if we can speak during the break, we can probably resolve that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We decide to admit into evidence exhibits number 890, 891 and 892, that is, the stipulations of the parties. As regards the document 884A and B and documents 877, 78, and 79, will be discussed together with other documents that the Chamber needs to rule upon. And the document 165 will perhaps have to wait until the close of the day today so that we can make a ruling in respect of that document as well. So you have heard the ruling of the Chamber regarding your documents, and now I think that we can now proceed with the rejoinder of the Defence in this case. Mr. Petrusic, are you in a position to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. The Defence is ready to proceed with this phase of the proceedings. We have a witness waiting, and in view of that, I should like to propose that we move into private session briefly because the witness will be requesting protective measures. We have discussed the issue with the counsel from the Prosecution, and they agree as regards the protective measures, that is, the pseudonym and image distortion of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move into private session so that we can hear about the reasons for this application for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. DG, were you a member of the army of Republika Srpska, and if so, during which period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member from the 7th of July, 1993, to 1995. I'm not sure of the exact date.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During the war on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were a regular soldier doing your regular military service, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: What training did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was an encrypter, radio telegraphy, signalsman.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: In the period, that is to say, at the beginning of July 1995 up until -- or rather, throughout July, were you within the composition of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: During that time, did you perform the duties for which you were trained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: May I just ask you to make pauses between my question and your answer. We, of course, speak the same language, but what we say has to be interpreted, so let us try to make greater pauses between question and answer to facilitate the work of the interpreters. Thank you. Witness DG, can you explain to us, please, briefly what your work consisted of, that is to say, your professional training and your work as an encrypter and teleprinter operator.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would receive telegrams, encrypt them, and decode them.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Would you explain to us the technique you used, how were telegrams received, how you decoded them, and your role in that work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A telegram would come from the operative centre to the office of the encrypter. It was placed at a small aperture that existed in the office, and the encrypter would take over the telegram and process it on the teleprinter. After that, he would encode this on a special machine, a machine -- an encryption machine, and once the message has been encrypted, he would hand it over to the teleprinter operator and he would dispatch it further to the addressee where the telegram was intended to go.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You're now talking about the premises you worked in, the office you worked in. Now, I am interested in knowing whether you can do the same kind of work in -- on the terrain, in the field, where you don't have your office, and if so, how you go about your business in the field, on location, as it were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can do my work in the field, but you have to have a special vehicle with all the devices in it which is supplied with the antenna in order to be able to establish communication with the station in question.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: From the 5th of July up until the 11th of July, were you at the forward command post of Pribicevac, doing the work you have just described to us, that is to say, working as an encrypter and teleprinter operator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You performed your work in the vehicle that you have just described to us; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When did you leave the forward command post of Pribicevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left Pribicevac when the army entered Srebrenica. I don't remember the exact date, but I do know that when the army passed the centre of town and went further on, we received orders from Major Jevdjevic, we packed up our things and went towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what time of the day it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was between 6.30 and 7.30.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Witness DG, the event that you're talking about, the entry of the army into Srebrenica, and what among the parties in the trial is not contested is the date, the 11th of July. Yes, when you spoke about the time of day, 6.30 -- between 6.30 and 7.30, you mean the afternoon, p.m.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you describe briefly for us the route you took and what your destination was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Pribicevac, that's when we left Pribicevac at that time, as I say, between 6.30 and 7.30 p.m., we came across a downhill section, a steep slope, and the Major ordered us to get out of the vehicle because the slope was so steep that there was the fear that it would turn over, and even the driver had to keep his door open for this eventuality, in case it started turning over, that he could jump out. After that, we reached an asphalt road with sharp bends, and that was our descent towards Srebrenica, down this asphalt road with the sharp bends.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And then you continued your journey through Srebrenica towards where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stopped in Srebrenica. We stopped for three, four, five minutes. We got out of the vehicle. Some of my friends wanted to take a television set because we didn't have a television set in our -- in the room we slept in. But the Major ordered us not to do that and he said that nobody was allowed to take anything except the driver who took up a shovel because we needed a shovel for our vehicle. We didn't have a shovel. The Major also took a potted plant. He took that with him, a pot with flowers, and we went on towards Bratunac in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. DG, without going into the details, tell us, please, along that road to Bratunac, did you pass Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you notice anything characteristic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we passed through Srebrenica. When the doors opened, were opened in Potocari, I saw, I noticed a UN base. And before that, when I opened the door, I saw a mass of people. When I opened the door again at one point, on the right-hand side of the road, I saw the UN base and on the left-hand side, I saw the large UN hangars. Beside that, there was a small stone church where the dome of the church had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Tell me Mr. DG, when did you arrive in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was already dark. I don't know exactly, but we -- it started getting dark as we were passing through Srebrenica, which means that it might have been at around 10.00 p.m., half past 9.00 or 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but it was between half an hour to one hour.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: And where did your route take you after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Major ordered that nobody was to leave the vehicle, and when he returned, we went on towards Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Tell us, please, at the end of that journey, your destination was Vlasenica, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but it was around 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask the usher to take up Defence Exhibit D80.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. DG, whether this is your signature on this telegram.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Tell me, please, briefly, what does your handwritten note mean at the bottom of this telegram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I received the telegram at 5.35, and that I sent it or handed it over to somebody in the operations centre five minutes later, five minutes after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, could we see on the ELMO the original, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence was just going to suggest that. Could you please place the original of the document that the witness has under the ELMO so that his signature can be seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but I think we have a problem of -- involving the protection of the witness. It's not legible, that's true. Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So Mr. DG, you received this dispatch at 1715, gave it a number, and then handed it in to the operations centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can remove the document from the ELMO now.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. DG, was it your duty to deliver that telegram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So every telegram that you received, it was your duty to deliver it in person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
